tagline: Red pine stands give way to lakes and marshes along Highway 46
intro: The Avenue of Pines follows Highway 46 between Deer River and Northome through forest, lakes and marshes. Explore Minnesota lists the scenic byway as 46 miles and singles out mature red pine stands and the changing breadth of the views. Within the pines the view is enclosed; near the lakes and marshes it opens out. The route passes through the Chippewa National Forest, with Lake Winnibigoshish and Cut Foot Sioux among the waters along the corridor. Aspen and birch accompany the pines in the state tourism office’s description of the forest scenery along the route.

Highway 46 was authorized in 1933, but its paving came in stages. A gravel section remained in the middle of the route in 1953; by 1958 the entire road was paved. The road’s two ends also have logging histories: prisoners of war worked at a camp near Deer River late in World War II, while Northome had grown as a logging town early in the century.

Start at US 2 near Deer River and follow Highway 46 northwest. The lake country includes Winnibigoshish and Cut Foot Sioux before the road continues through Squaw Lake. Farther north, Alvwood and then Bergville lead toward Northome, where Highway 46 ends at Highway 1.
notice: Enclosed views through the pines open out near lakes and marshes.

moments.title: Deer River
moments.text: Near Deer River, a former CCC camp became a logging camp staffed by prisoners of war late in World War II. The town’s lumber history also included a superintendent’s house built in 1904 for the Itasca Lumber Company. Highway 46 begins near Deer River at US 2, making the town the southern gateway to the drive through the national forest.

moments.title: Lake Winnibigoshish
moments.text: The Mississippi flows through Lake Winnibigoshish, a 67,000-acre lake in the Chippewa National Forest. At its outlet, the Army Corps of Engineers built a dam from 1881 to 1884 to regulate the Upper Mississippi’s flow. Loggers, fur traders and millers downstream at St. Anthony Falls wanted a steady supply of water. The dam history records a 14-foot rise in water level and destruction of Ojibwa homes and fisheries along the shores. A replacement built in 1899 substituted concrete for wooden components. The dam stands at the lake’s outlet to the Mississippi, within the Leech Lake Indian Reservation.

moments.title: Cut Foot Sioux Lake
moments.text: Williams Narrows, a channel 100 feet wide, connects Cut Foot Sioux Lake to the larger Lake Winnibigoshish. The lake also lies along the Cut Foot Sioux Trail, a 22-mile loop using gravel and sand forestry roads. From the visitor information center on Highway 46, the trail runs west through woods past lakes, including Cut Foot Sioux. It connects with the Simpson Creek Trail system through large red pines on a peninsula extending into Winnibigoshish. The connected trail route passes through the Cut Foot Experimental Forest, where researchers study pine forest management.
